---
description: "How NCodeGroup C# code allocates, rents, sizes, copies, owns and disposes buffers, collections and disposable resources, with extra care for secret material and untrusted input."
applyTo: "**/*.cs"
---

# Allocations and buffers

<!-- Generated by `npm run train` from the sources each rule cites. To change a rule for good, change its source or say so in training/feedback.md; the next training run regenerates this file. -->

- **When you compute a byte count from an element count and an element size, for example to call `CryptographicOperations.ZeroMemory` over `MemoryMarshal.AsBytes` of a generic or wide span, process the span in chunks of at most `int.MaxValue / Unsafe.SizeOf<T>()` elements.** The multiplication can overflow `int`. A checked overflow throws before anything is zeroed, which leaves the secret in memory and breaks large buffers that `Span<T>.Clear()` used to handle. *Check:* Look for `checked(length * elementSize)`, `length * Unsafe.SizeOf<T>()`, or `MemoryMarshal.AsBytes` over a whole span of generic or wide elements with no chunking. Check that a test covers the chunked path. <sub>Buffers outcomes of #75</sub>
- **Hold secret material (passwords and their decoded or normalized copies, content-encryption and key-encryption keys, shared secrets, private key and PEM bytes, decrypted payloads) only in sensitive pooled rentals, such as `NCode.Buffers` `BufferFactory.Rent(..., isSensitive: true, ...)` or `SecureMemoryPool`, which are pinned and zeroed on return. This includes the fallback used when the data is too large for `stackalloc`. Dispose each rental as soon as the operation is done, and never turn secret bytes into a `string`.** Strings and ordinary arrays can't be reliably wiped and may be copied by the GC. A pinned GC array that is wiped by hand sits outside the secure pool, and every exception path has to remember to wipe it. *Check:* Look for secret bytes in `new byte[]`, `GC.AllocateUninitializedArray(..., pinned: true)`, non-sensitive or `ArrayPool` rentals returned without clearing, `Encoding.GetBytes(password)` into plain arrays, `File.ReadAllText`/`ReadAllBytes` of private keys, secret data written to non-sensitive pooled writers, and rentals kept after the hash, verify, sign or unwrap call has finished. <sub>Identity ADR-1230; Identity ADR-1235; Identity ADR-1238; Identity ADR-1409; Identity docs/backend-for-frontend.md; Identity outcomes of #532; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity review of #420</sub>
- **When a method writes output whose length the caller can't know in advance, such as an unwrapped or decrypted key whose size only a remote service's response reveals, take an `IBufferWriter<byte>` destination. Advance the writer only after the operation succeeds, and zero whatever was written if it fails. Keep a `Span<byte>` destination with an `out int` count only for results of known size.** Callers who must guess a size over-rent or fail with "destination too small" instead of reaching their own size check. A failed or partial write must not leave secret bytes in the writer. *Check:* Look at unwrap, decrypt and key-agreement APIs, especially async or interface methods backed by a service. Flag a variable-length result returned as a fresh `byte[]` or written to a fixed `Memory<byte>`/`Span<byte>`, a call to `Advance` before the operation succeeds, bytes left uncleared on an exception path, and callers that over-rent to work around the API. <sub>Identity ADR-1260; Identity review of #370; Identity ADR-1474</sub>
- **Send requests to untrusted endpoints with `HttpCompletionOption.ResponseHeadersRead`. Read the body only through a capped reader that enforces a hard byte limit while it streams, rents its read chunk from a pool, and treats `Content-Length` only as a hint. Parse the capped body straight from the written buffer or sequence, without copying it into an intermediate array or string.** The pipeline's timeouts end once the headers arrive, so an uncapped body read lets a remote server exhaust resources, and a missing or false length must not get around the cap. Extra copies waste the allocation the capped read avoids. *Check:* Flag `ReadAsStringAsync`, `ReadAsByteArrayAsync`, `ReadFromJsonAsync` or an uncapped `ReadAsStreamAsync` copy on an untrusted response, caps that trust `Content-Length`, and `.ToArray()`, `Encoding.GetString` or `MemoryStream` copies made before parsing. <sub>Identity ADR-1315</sub>
- **When you pre-size a collection or buffer from a length read from peer-supplied data (a CBOR array or map header, a length prefix), clamp the capacity to what the remaining input bytes could actually hold.** The declared length is controlled by the attacker, so an unclamped capacity such as 2^31-1 lets a tiny message force a huge allocation. *Check:* Look for `new List<T>(n)`, `new Dictionary<K,V>(n)` or a rental where `n` comes from a decoded header. Check that it is bounded by the remaining bytes (for example, half of them for maps) and that a test feeds in an oversized declared length. <sub>Identity outcomes of #554</sub>
- **Split fixed-segment input with `MemoryExtensions.Split` into a `stackalloc Range[expected + 1]` buffer, and reject any count other than `expected`.** Without the spare slot, extra segments fold into the last range and pass validation. `string.Split` also allocates. *Check:* Look for `string.Split` on fixed-format input, and for `Range` buffers sized exactly to the expected count. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, when a callback inside `string.Create` passes the character writing to another implementation, verify that the count written equals `chars.Length`, and pass span inputs through an `internal readonly ref struct` state.** A short write would persist a `'\0'` remainder in the string. Ref-struct state passes spans without copying them. *Check:* Look for `string.Create` callbacks that pass the writing to another method and don't verify `WrittenCount == chars.Length`. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **A type or in-process store that keeps caller-supplied bytes (`ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`, `Memory<byte>` or an array) stores its own copy, not the caller's memory. A public operation that takes borrowed memory documents whether it reads or copies the value before its returned task completes.** A caller that reuses or returns a pooled buffer would otherwise change stored values. Without the documented guarantee, a caller can't tell when it may release its rental. *Check:* Look for constructors, stores or setters that assign a memory or array parameter directly to a field. Look also for public methods taking `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` whose docs don't say whether the buffer may be reused after the call, and for rented memory passed to async writes whose interface doesn't document that the value is copied. <sub>Identity ADR-1164; coordination outcomes of #17; Identity review of #420</sub>
- **In production code, copy every collection a type stores, including an injected `IEnumerable<T>`, once into a collection it owns, chosen by how it is used: `FrozenDictionary`/`FrozenSet` for repeated lookups, `ImmutableArray<T>` or an array (`[.. x]`, `.ToArray()`) for iteration, and `List<T>` only for a set that really is mutated.** A stored caller collection can change underneath the type, or be enumerated lazily again on every use. *Check:* Look for constructors, methods or setters that assign a collection or `IEnumerable<T>` parameter directly to a field or property. *Note:* Test projects are exempt. For example, a private sealed nested stub that one test file needs may keep what it is given. <sub>Identity convention-audit.instructions.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, dispose every `HttpResponseMessage`, `Stream` and `IHttpClientFactory`-created `HttpClient` the code owns, including each response that retry logic discards before the next attempt.** An undisposed response or stream holds its connection and buffers. *Check:* Look for results of `SendAsync`/`GetAsync`, opened streams and factory-created clients with no `using` or `Dispose`, and for retry loops or `OnRetry` callbacks that drop the previous response without disposing it. <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1336</sub>
- **Dispose a disposable client, credential or certificate that a cache drops (it lost a `GetOrAdd` race, was evicted or was released), but never while a call or HTTP handler may still be using it. Keep certificates used by handlers in a singleton cache that disposes them when the container is disposed.** Dropped clients hold sockets until finalization, and retries can exhaust connections. Disposing a certificate under a live handler breaks its handshakes. *Check:* Look at `GetOrAdd` races, `TryRemove`, eviction and release paths on caches of disposable objects. Look also for certificates handed to handlers that are disposed in a `using`, evicted, or left with no owner. <sub>Identity outcomes of #584; Identity ADR-1300</sub>
- **Don't ask a component to dispose a replaced cached `X509Certificate2Collection` on rotation when operations in flight on other threads may still hold the old reference and nothing counts references.** Disposing it would break a chain build in flight on another request. The certificates hold nothing their finalizers don't release, and rotation is rare. *Check:* Before reporting a leaked certificate collection on reload, check whether concurrent readers can still hold the old reference. <sub>Identity outcomes of #794</sub>
- **When a request needs a client certificate in more than one place, decode it once per request and cache it in the request's items. Dispose the certificates you decoded when the request ends, and never dispose `HttpContext.Connection.ClientCertificate`.** Every consumer must see the same certificate. The connection's certificate belongs to the connection, not to the request. *Check:* Look for the certificate header decoded again by each consumer, for decoded `X509Certificate2` instances that are never disposed or registered for disposal with the response, and for disposal of the connection's certificate. <sub>Identity ADR-1172</sub>
- **When data built in a span or a pooled buffer has to survive an `await`, keep it in a pooled `Memory<T>` lease that is held across the await and returned (with `using` or `finally`) once the call finishes. Don't copy it with `ToArray()`, and don't restructure the code to try to keep a span alive.** A span can't be held across an `await`, and a `ToArray()` copy adds a heap allocation to every operation. *Check:* Look in async methods for `lease.Span.ToArray()` or `.Memory.ToArray()` results that are only passed to an awaited call, and for leases returned before the awaited call completes. <sub>Identity ADR-1472; Identity outcomes of #702</sub>
- **Don't report a `ToArray()` copy of caller-supplied memory that is passed to a client command the code may abandon (through `WaitAsync` or cancellation) while the client may still send it later.** An abandoned command may be sent after the caller's buffer has been returned or reused, so the command needs an array it owns. *Check:* Before flagging the copy, look for a comment explaining it, for abandonment through `WaitAsync` or cancellation, and for sibling methods that also pass arrays they built. <sub>Identity outcomes of #460</sub>
- **Read and write a defined little-endian wire encoding with `BinaryPrimitives`, not by reinterpreting memory with `MemoryMarshal.Cast` or `Unsafe.As`. Use `MemoryMarshal.Cast<byte, T>` only for limbs with a byte-aligned radix (for example, not radix-2^51).** Reinterpreting memory depends on the host's endianness, and it matches the wire format only when limbs are byte-aligned. *Check:* Look for `MemoryMarshal.Cast` or `Unsafe.As` used to serialize wire data or limbs that aren't byte-aligned. <sub>Identity ADR-1266</sub>
- **When you view a struct with fields of one blittable type as a span through `MemoryMarshal.CreateSpan(ref Unsafe.As<TStruct, TField>(ref value), count)`, cover the struct with round-trip tests that verify its sequential layout.** The view relies on the struct's sequential layout, and only tests catch a change to it. *Check:* Flag a new struct span view that has no matching round-trip test. <sub>Identity ADR-1266</sub>
- **Convert a DER ECDSA signature to fixed-width r‖s, each half `(KeySizeBits + 7) / 8` bytes, with a strict parser built on `AsnDecoder`, and hash the signing input into a rental whose sensitivity is given explicitly.** Strict parsing rejects malformed signatures, a wrong half width produces invalid signatures, and the rental keeps signing off the allocation path. *Check:* Look for hand-rolled or lenient DER parsing, a wrong half width, or a digest allocated as a new array. <sub>Identity ADR-1474</sub>
- **In production code, have a producer of binary output (crypto, encoding, serialization, signatures, public keys) write into a caller-supplied `Span<byte>`, `IBufferWriter<byte>`, `ref TWriter` (`where TWriter : IBufferWriter<byte>, allows ref struct`) or `Utf8JsonWriter`, and offer a sizing method alongside it where the length is computable. Take `ReadOnlySpan<byte>`/`ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` inputs, and don't return or take `byte[]`. Async remote operations write into caller-supplied `Memory<byte>` and return `ValueTask<int>`.** Returning arrays allocates on every call and forces the caller to copy. A caller-supplied destination lets the caller choose a stack, pooled or sensitive buffer. *Check:* Flag new methods that return `byte[]` or `Task<byte[]>` (including `SerializeToUtf8Bytes` or `ToArray()` results), or that take `byte[]` parameters for binary data. *Note:* See the exception for non-secret wire encoders whose array return is recorded in an ADR. <sub>Identity ADR-1235; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity review of #382; Identity review of #420; Randomness outcomes of #13; Identity ADR-1474</sub>
- **Don't ask a token or message encoder that returns a new `byte[]` to write to a caller-supplied buffer writer when its output is non-secret wire data that the caller keeps or sends whole, and an ADR or the sibling encoders set that array-return convention.** Such output is like a compact token returned as a string, so a pooled or sensitive destination adds nothing. *Check:* Before reporting an array return on an encode or issue API, check whether the output is secret and whether an ADR or the sibling encoders record the array-returning design. <sub>Identity outcomes of #554</sub>
- **In production code, rent transient byte buffers that live only for the call: use a `NCode.Buffers` `BufferFactory` rental or pooled buffer writer inside a `using`, `ArrayPool<byte>.Shared` with a return in `finally`, or a small fixed-size `stackalloc`. Use the sensitive variants for secrets or tokens. Use `new byte[]`, `.ToArray()`, `ArrayBufferWriter<T>` or `MemoryStream` only where an external API requires them, and then over a rented array obtained with `MemoryMarshal.TryGetArray` where possible.** Per-call arrays add GC pressure, and large ones land on the large object heap. Pooled buffers avoid the allocation, and the sensitive variants clear secrets when returned. *Check:* Flag a local `new byte[n]`, `GC.AllocateArray`, `ArrayBufferWriter<byte>`, `MemoryStream`/`ToArray()` or `SerializeToUtf8Bytes` result that is neither returned nor stored and is used only as scratch space, for example between serializing and re-parsing. *Note:* Test projects are exempt from this production rule. <sub>Identity ADR-1235; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity review of #316; Identity review of #382; Identity review of #420; Identity ADR-1283; Randomness outcomes of #12; Randomness outcomes of #13</sub>
- **Use the span and destination overloads for transient results that are used once: `HashData(source, destination)` into a `stackalloc` span, `Encoding.GetBytes(ReadOnlySpan<char>, Span<byte>)`, `Convert.TryFromBase64String`, and `Convert.FromHexString(ReadOnlySpan<char>, Span<byte>, ...)` straight into the destination. Hash concatenated parts with `IncrementalHash` instead of building an array or string first, and encode text straight into the destination writer.** The array-returning overloads, and arrays or strings built only to be hashed or copied onward, add avoidable allocations on every call. *Check:* Look for `HashData(x)`, `GetBytes(string)`, `Convert.FromBase64String`, `FromHexString(string)` or interpolated strings whose result is used once (hashed, copied into a writer) and then dropped. <sub>Identity review of #420; Randomness outcomes of #12; Randomness outcomes of #13; Identity outcomes of #692</sub>
- **Don't report an exactly sized array allocation when the array outlives the call: it is stored in a field or property of a returned or stored object, or it is a size-capped response body that callers keep, cache or parse whole. Only the transient pieces, such as the read chunk, need to be rented. Don't demand a second, pooled read path next to a shared capped read that allocates once per uncached operation.** A rented buffer can't live in an object that outlives the call, so one exact allocation there is intentional. An extra read path costs more complexity than it saves. *Check:* Before reporting an allocation, check whether the array is returned, stored or cached, whether the read is capped and shared, whether the read chunk is already rented, and how often the code runs. <sub>Identity review of #420; Randomness outcomes of #12; Randomness outcomes of #13</sub>
- **Don't ask for a value that isn't a credential (such as a lease-ownership nonce) to be encoded into a rented, zeroed buffer when the same bytes are already stored elsewhere in plaintext or copied by the code that receives them. Don't use a secure encoding helper (such as `SecureEncoding`) for text that isn't sensitive.** Zeroing gains no secrecy when copies already exist, and it keeps a rental alive across awaits. The secure encoding is meant for sensitive text only. *Check:* Before reporting an unpooled or unzeroed encoding, confirm that the value really is secret and that no other plaintext copy exists. Flag `SecureEncoding.*.GetBytes` on non-sensitive text. <sub>Identity outcomes of #460; Identity outcomes of #692</sub>
- **In production code, when a consumer needs one contiguous span of a `Sequence<T>` or `ReadOnlySequence<T>` (a cryptographic primitive, a base64url codec), take `GetSpanLease(isSensitive:)`. Any other consumer reads segment by segment or with `SequenceReader<T>`. Never concatenate segments by hand or call `.ToArray()`.** The lease returns a single segment without copying, and otherwise returns a pooled copy with the right sensitivity. Other copies waste memory and may leave secret copies behind. *Check:* Look for `ReadOnlySequence<T>.ToArray()`, loops that copy segments into a new array, and contiguous consumers that don't use `GetSpanLease`. <sub>Identity ADR-1266; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1315</sub>
- **Read JSON back with `JsonElement.Parse`, not `JsonDocument`, and back an immutable JSON-wrapping type with a detached `JsonElement` that owns no `JsonDocument`.** A detached element leaves nothing to dispose and nothing to clone defensively. *Check:* Look for `JsonDocument.Parse` used to read a record, and for wrapper types that hold a `JsonDocument` field, implement `IDisposable` only to free it, or clone on every access. <sub>Identity ADR-1283; Identity ADR-1119</sub>
- **In production code, use the buffer from `NCode.Buffers` `BufferFactory.Rent` at the length it returns, without slicing it back to the requested length. Prefer the `out Span<T>` overload, and take `out Memory<T>` only for a buffer stored in a field or used across an `await`.** The rented buffer already has exactly the requested length, sensitive or not. A span is cheaper when memory isn't needed. *Check:* Look for `.Slice(0, length)` or `[..length]` on a `BufferFactory.Rent` result, and for `out Memory<T>` used only synchronously within one method. *Note:* Don't report a missing slice after `BufferFactory.Rent`. Only raw `ArrayPool<T>.Rent` and `MemoryPool<T>.Rent` return oversized buffers that need slicing. <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #807</sub>
- **In production code, a helper that rents and fills a buffer for its caller returns the lease plus a read-only view: `out ReadOnlySpan<T>`, or `out ReadOnlyMemory<T>` across an `await`.** Only the rent call itself should hand back writable memory. Consumers shouldn't modify filled output. *Check:* Look for helpers that return a lease with `out Span<T>` or `out Memory<T>` over data they have already filled. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, create a `string` only for a non-secret value at a storage or wire boundary, exactly once, written in place with `string.Create`. Never fill a rented `char` buffer and then copy it out with `new string(span)` or `.ToString()`.** The copy adds an allocation and an extra pass. *Check:* Look for `ArrayPool<char>` rentals followed by `new string(...)` or `AsSpan().ToString()`, and for repeated intermediate strings on hot paths. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1235</sub>
- **Expose a fixed byte label used on every call as `static ReadOnlySpan<byte> Label => "..."u8;`, not as a `const string` encoded on each call.** Encoding a constant on every call allocates and wastes work. *Check:* Look for a `const string` passed through `Encoding.*.GetBytes` on a hot path. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Pass array-backed `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` to an SDK that takes arrays through `MemoryMarshal.TryGetArray`, and copy only when the SDK needs an array of exactly the data's length.** This avoids a needless copy on every call. *Check:* Look for `ToArray()` on memory handed to an SDK where `TryGetArray` would give the segment directly. <sub>Identity ADR-1474</sub>
- **Parse and validate strings with `ReadOnlySpan<char>` slices, `MemoryExtensions.Split` ranges and span `StartsWith`/`Equals`, not with `string.Split`, `Substring` or helpers that return new strings.** Span slicing allocates no substrings or arrays. *Check:* Look for `.Split(`, `.Substring(` or private helpers returning `string` slices in validation or parsing code. <sub>Identity review of #420</sub>
- **Don't ask a method that only reads text to take `ReadOnlySpan<char>` instead of `string` when its callers already hold whole strings. The span-input convention is for byte inputs.** Callers that pass whole strings gain nothing from the change. *Check:* Before reporting a `string` parameter that is only read, check whether callers pass whole strings or would have to allocate substrings to call it. *Note:* An earlier review (Identity #341) asked for `ReadOnlySpan<char>` on helpers that only read text, while keeping public contract properties as `string`. That still applies where callers would otherwise slice with `Substring`. The more specific later rule wins when callers hold strings. <sub>coordination outcomes of #31; Identity review of #341</sub>
- **Give a `List`, `Dictionary` or `HashSet` an initial capacity when the final size or an upper bound is known, using the smaller of the bound and the source count when the bound can be large. Return a shared empty instance (`Array.Empty<T>()`, `FrozenSet<T>.Empty`, or `[]` typed as `IEnumerable<T>`/`IReadOnlyList<T>`) for an empty result. Create a collection that is usually empty lazily (`(failures ??= []).Add(ex)`), and write `list ?? (IReadOnlyCollection<T>)[]`, not `list ?? []`.** Unsized collections reallocate as they grow. `?? []` on a `List<T>` expression, and eagerly created empty lists, allocate on every call. *Check:* Look for `new List<T>()` or similar without a capacity when the count is at hand, `new List<T>()` or a `List<T>`-typed `[]` returned as an empty result on frequent read paths, `?? []` on a `List`-typed expression, and lists created at the start of a method only to collect rare items such as exceptions. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; coordination outcomes of #19; coordination outcomes of #20; coordination outcomes of #22; Randomness outcomes of #16</sub>
- **Don't report enumerator allocation in a `foreach` over an interface-typed collection when the loop isn't on a per-request path (for example, it runs once per session end) or when the empty case iterates a shared empty array.** The allocation-free loop rule targets per-request paths, and .NET returns a cached enumerator for an empty array. *Check:* Before reporting, check how often the loop runs and whether an empty result is the shared `Array.Empty` instance. <sub>coordination outcomes of #20</sub>
- **Don't report `.AsTask()` on `ValueTask`s that are collected for `Task.WhenAll`, or that are stored and awaited more than once, as a needless allocation.** `Task.WhenAll` needs tasks, and a `ValueTask` may be awaited only once, so the conversion is required. *Check:* Before reporting an `AsTask` allocation, check whether the tasks feed `Task.WhenAll` or are awaited more than once. <sub>coordination outcomes of #22</sub>
- **Choose between a stack buffer and a rented buffer in one conditional expression, and dispose the optional lease with a `using` declaration. Don't declare a placeholder such as `stackalloc byte[0]` just to satisfy an analyzer, and don't use a nullable lease local disposed in `try`/`finally`.** The placeholder and the `try`/`finally` are harder to read and depart from the house disposal style. *Check:* Look for `stackalloc byte[0]` that is later overwritten, analyzer suppressions next to it, and nullable lease locals disposed in `finally`. <sub>Identity outcomes of #552</sub>
- **Don't ask for a literal initial capacity passed to a growable pooled buffer writer (such as `BufferFactory.CreatePooledBufferWriter`) to become a named constant.** It is only a starting size that the writer grows past, not a limit. *Check:* Before reporting a magic number, check whether it is the initial-capacity argument of a growable buffer. <sub>Identity outcomes of #709</sub>
